Calibrated abstention in retrieval agents

November 13, 2025 Ada Example and Bo Placeholder, Research Scientists

We introduce calibrated abstention, a training recipe that teaches retrieval agents to decline a question when the retrieved evidence does not support any answer. The recipe pairs every training question with an evidence set that is deliberately incomplete for a fixed fraction of examples.

Agents trained this way abstain on most unsupported questions while answering nearly as many supported ones as the baseline. The effect holds across three evidence corpora and two model sizes, and it does not require any change to the retrieval component itself.

How the recipe works

For each question we sample an evidence set from the corpus and, with probability one in four, remove the passages that contain the answer. The agent is rewarded for answering correctly when the evidence suffices and for abstaining when it does not; a wrong answer is penalised more heavily than an abstention.

We measure calibration as the gap between the agent's stated confidence and its accuracy on the questions it chooses to answer. Trained agents halve this gap compared with prompting alone, and the gain persists when the corpus is swapped for one the agent never saw during training.

Limitations

Abstention is learned relative to the training corpus, so a corpus with systematically missing topics teaches the agent to abstain on those topics as well. We describe a simple rebalancing step that reduces this effect, and we release the evaluation sets so that others can measure it on their own corpora.
